newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Arrests made in Colombian "narco-jet" scandal.
newsitem.headline: Arrests made in Colombian "narco-jet" scandal.

text.p: Eleven Colombian Air Force personnel, including several officers, have been arrested in connection with the heroin found stashed aboard President Ernesto Samper's presidential jet, officials said on Sunday.

More than eight pounds (3.7 kg) of heroin were discovered aboard the Boeing 707 aircraft on Friday night as it was being readied at the Catam military air base on the outskirts of Bogota for a flight to New York, where Samper is to address the United Nations General Assembly on Monday.

The plane is owned and operated by the Colombian Air Force, and National Police chief Gen. Rosso Jose Serrano has said air force personnel were among prime suspects in the case dubbed the "narco-jet" scandal by the Colombian media.
Military and judicial officials said on Sunday that an air force colonel, a major, several captains and a sergeant were among the 11 people who had been arrested for questioning in the scandal.
All were being held incommunicado at Catam and questioned by investigators from the office of chief prosecutor Alfonso Valdivieso.
The 11 were all involved in a test flight of the 707 on Friday in which it flew from Bogota to the southwest city of Cali and then on to the northwest city of Medellin before returning to Catam.
Theories abound about how the heroin found its way aboard the plane, and about how it might have been part of a plot to further damage Samper's drug-tainted image abroad.
But Samper himself appeared to shrug off the scandal during his flight to New York on Saturday aboard a commercial jet chartered by Colombia's Avianca airlines.
"Thanks to Avianca we arrived safely and weighing a few kilos less," Samper quipped to reporters on board the flight.
"Now, because of the heroin, the presidential plane is going to be called the Policarpa Salavarrieta," he added, referring to a heroine of Colombia's war for independence from Spain.

According to Bogota's El Espectador newspaper, Samper also made light of the fact that the Avianca jet that took him to New York was named after Santiago de Cali, the historical figure Colombia's second-largest city takes its name from.

Samper's U.S. travel visa was revoked in July because of charges his 1994 election campaign was partly financed by the Cali drug cartel. The travel restriction does not affect heads of state visiting U.N. headquarters in New York.
